chapter: Porch interview and Jazz Train plans
title: The first song and the Ethel Waters Black Swan session
summary: At the end of a day of Black Swan recording the musicians left, so Johnson played for Ethel Waters with cloth to muffle the piano, his first record.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: What was the first song you ever wrote?
Oh, gosh. It was not too long ago, I guess (inaudible).
Ninety percent of them. They were all songwriters. See, I was in a group of songwriter during that time and I pulled together -- I organized (inaudible).
I didn't realize that you didn't --
I don't have my specs. What is that?
All right, this is a slice of (inaudible) bread in the brown sack, a quart of milk.
A quart of milk, all right.
Ethel Waters recorded the first song you ever wrote.

Yeah, yeah, she did. And it's a nice story. It goes a long way back. Had the recording because -- out in Long Island, out to the Black Swan Restaurant. (Inaudible) had been making records all day. And so when they finished, I -- none of the musicians would stay to record with us.

No, they were tired (inaudible). So, Ethel said, well, J.C., we've been here all day, you play it. (Inaudible.) I've never made a record. So, said, okay, so I started to play, like this, you could hear every beat on the record because they had big things that looked like wax. It was a big (inaudible). So I began to play (inaudible). So they went and got a lot of pieces of cloth and everything they could find to put down (inaudible).
So I finally made the record with her. And it came out (inaudible). The first record I ever made was
Do you have that record from your --
Uh-huh. I'd like to hear it someday.
